title: Question 11
stem:
A photon of wavelength $540\text{ nm}$ collides with an isolated stationary electron, as illustrated in Fig. 11.1.

{{figure:figure_11_1}}

The photon is deflected elastically by the electron.
The wavelength of the deflected photon is $544\text{ nm}$.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State what is meant by a photon.
hints: Hint 1: Think about how electromagnetic energy travels - does it arrive as a smooth continuous flow, or in tiny discrete bundles?
Hint 2: Focus on the two key words needed: what name is given to a discrete packet, and what family of waves does light belong to?
parts.proper_answer: A photon is a discrete quantum (packet) of energy of electromagnetic radiation.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Light Really Is**
You know light can behave like a wave, but it also arrives in little lumps of energy. We call each lump a quantum. So start by thinking of a photon not as a tiny hard ball, but as one packet of energy.

Step 2: **Complete The Definition**
That packet belongs specifically to electromagnetic waves. So a full definition is: $$ \text{photon = quantum of energy of e.m. radiation} $$ Its energy is given by $E = hf = hc/\lambda$.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: On Fig. 11.1, draw an arrow to indicate the approximate direction of motion of the deflected electron.

markscheme_points.text: arrow (on Fig. 11.1) pointing upwards and to the right

hints: Hint 1: Think about momentum as vectors. The incident photon moves right, the deflected photon gains a downward component, so which way must the electron go to keep total momentum balanced?
parts.proper_answer: Arrow starting at the collision point directed approximately upwards and to the right, so that transverse momentum is conserved.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Momentum Conservation**
Total momentum must be conserved in both x and y directions. Initially everything is along the incident direction to the right, with zero momentum up or down.

Step 2: **Balance The Sideways Kick**
The deflected photon in Fig. 11.1 goes down and to the right, so it carries downward momentum. The electron must therefore carry upward momentum to cancel it. It must also move forward to the right to help conserve forward momentum. So draw an arrow from the electron position pointing up and to the right.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: the momentum of the deflected photon
hints: Hint 1: Think about which wave property of the deflected photon you are given and which universal constant links its particle-like momentum to that wave property.
Hint 2: Check your units before calculating - the wavelength must be in metres, so convert 544 nm to $10^{-9}$ m form first.
parts.proper_answer: $p = 1.22 \times 10^{-27} \text{ N s}$ along direction of deflected photon.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Momentum To Wavelength**
Even though a photon has no mass, it carries momentum. Its wave and particle natures are linked by the Planck constant $h$: $$ p = \frac{h}{\lambda} $$ Use the deflected wavelength $\lambda = 544 \text{ nm}$.

Step 2: **Convert And Calculate**
First convert to SI: $$ \lambda = 544 \text{ nm} = 544 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m} $$ Then with $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$: $$ p = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{544 \times 10^{-9}} = 1.22 \times 10^{-27} \text{ N s} $$ This is the magnitude of momentum of the deflected photon.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: the energy transferred to the deflected electron.
hints: Hint 1: Think about where the electron's kinetic energy comes from - it must equal the energy lost by the photon when its wavelength increases from 540 nm to 544 nm.
Hint 2: Plan to find the energy of each photon separately using its wavelength in metres, then subtract final from initial to get the transfer.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Energy Lost By Photon = Energy Gained By Electron**
The collision is elastic, so total energy is conserved. The photon energy is: $$ E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} $$ A longer wavelength means less energy, so the difference goes to the electron.

Step 2: **Calculate The Difference**
$$ \Delta E = hc\left(\frac{1}{\lambda_{incident}} - \frac{1}{\lambda_{deflected}}\right) $$ $$ \Delta E = (6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3.00 \times 10^{8})\left(\frac{1}{540 \times 10^{-9}} - \frac{1}{544 \times 10^{-9}}\right) $$ $$ \Delta E = 2.7 \times 10^{-21} \text{ J} $$ This very small energy is the kinetic energy transferred to the initially stationary electron.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
Another photon of wavelength $540\text{ nm}$ collides with an isolated stationary electron.

Explain why it is not possible for the deflected photon to have a wavelength less than $540\text{ nm}$.

markscheme_points.text: (smaller wavelength corresponds to) greater photon energy

any one point from: (deflected) photon loses energy (so not possible); (deflected) photon would need to gain energy (so not possible); electron would need to lose energy (so not possible); initially electron energy is zero (so not possible)

hints: Hint 1: Think about how photon energy changes with wavelength - if the deflected wavelength were smaller than 540 nm, would the photon have gained or lost energy?
Hint 2: Think about whether the initially stationary electron can supply extra energy to the photon, given it starts with zero kinetic energy.
parts.proper_answer: Smaller wavelength corresponds to greater photon energy. The deflected photon cannot have gained energy because the initially stationary electron has zero kinetic energy to give, and energy must be conserved.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Shorter Wavelength Means More Energy**
From $E = hc/\lambda$, $E$ is inversely proportional to $\lambda$. A deflected wavelength $< 540 \text{ nm}$ would mean the photon leaves with more energy than it arrived with.

Step 2: **Why That Is Impossible Here**
That extra energy would have to come from the electron. But the electron is initially stationary, so its kinetic energy is zero - it has nothing to give. It can only gain energy, not lose it. Therefore the photon can only lose energy and shift to longer wavelength, as in Compton scattering, never to shorter wavelength.
